scenes.title: Where and when
narration: La Bamba originated in the late 17th century in Veracruz, Mexico, as a son jarocho folk song and dance.
It initially satirized the late and ineffective defense efforts against pirates by the Mexican viceroy.
The earliest known recording is by Álvaro Hernández Ortiz in 1938.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The music is son jarocho style, typically played on one or two arpa jarochas (harps), jarana jarocha (small guitar), and requinto jarocho (four-string guitar).
The harp has 39 strings and plays rapid arpeggios matching the dancers’ footwork.
Listen for the Arpa jarocha (harp), Jarana jarocha (small guitar), Requinto jarocho (four-string guitar).
The pulse is Binary meter.
Bright harp arpeggios intertwine with rhythmic guitar strumming and lively vocals, driven by a fast, binary rhythm that mirrors the dancers’ energetic footwork.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Álvaro Hernández Ortiz recorded the earliest known version in 1938.
Ritchie Valens popularized the song internationally in 1958 with a rock and roll version.
Variations exist within Veracruz, including differences in tempo and lyrical style.
La Bamba belongs to the son jarocho tradition, which blends Spanish, indigenous, and African musical and dance elements.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: La Bamba is parent of Son Jarocho: La Bamba is a key example of the son jarocho musical and dance tradition from Veracruz.
La Bamba is shares music of Bamba (Spanish dance): The name and some rhythmic elements may relate to the Spanish dance called Bamba popular in the 17th century.
La Bamba is influence of Bambara dance: Possible African influence via the Bambara people, linked through the transatlantic slave trade.
